paper.title: Attention Is All You Need
paper.venue: 31st Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NIPS 2017), Long Beach, CA, USA

evidence.thesis: Sequence transduction does not require recurrence or convolution: the Transformer, built on attention alone, reaches higher BLEU on two machine translation tasks while being far more parallelisable and markedly cheaper to train.
evidence.plainSummary: Until 2017 the standard for machine translation was the recurrent network, which processes words one after another. That sequential dependency is what made training hard to parallelise. This paper removes recurrence and convolution entirely and puts attention in their place. Inside every layer each position can look directly at every other; order is supplied separately, by sinusoidal position encodings added to the input embeddings. The result: 28.4 BLEU on WMT 2014 English-to-German, more than 2 BLEU above the previous best including ensembles, at a small fraction of their training cost. The paper also shows the architecture generalises to English constituency parsing without task-specific tuning. The trade-off is stated plainly: the cost of self-attention grows with the square of the sequence length.
evidence.researchQuestion: If recurrent and convolutional layers are removed from a sequence transduction model and replaced entirely by attention, what happens to translation quality, parallelisability and training cost?
methods: Encoder and decoder were each built as a stack of six identical layers, with every sub-layer wrapped in a residual connection followed by layer normalisation.
The attention function is Scaled Dot-Product Attention: query-key dot products are divided by √d_k before the softmax.
Instead of a single attention, h = 8 parallel heads are used, each operating at d_k = d_v = 64.
Masking in the decoder ensures position i can depend only on known outputs at positions before i, preserving the auto-regressive property.
Order information is injected through sine and cosine functions of different frequencies, added to the learned embeddings.
Each layer contains a position-wise feed-forward network with a ReLU in between two linear transformations (d_model = 512, d_ff = 2048).
Training ran on one machine with 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs, using Adam with a custom learning rate schedule that warms up over 4000 steps.
Regularisation combined residual dropout (P_drop = 0.1) with label smoothing of 0.1.
Models were trained on WMT 2014 English-German (about 4.5M sentence pairs) and English-French (36M sentences); beam search was used at inference.
The contribution of each component was measured through ablations on the newstest2013 development set, varying head count, d_k, model size, dropout and position encoding.
Generalisation was probed by training a 4-layer Transformer for English constituency parsing on the Penn Treebank WSJ portion.
findings: Transformer (big) reached 28.4 BLEU on WMT 2014 English-to-German, beating the previous best results — including ensembles — by more than 2 BLEU.
Table 2 lists 41.8 BLEU for the big model on English-to-French, obtained after 3.5 days of training on eight GPUs.
Even the base model surpassed every previously published model and ensemble, at an estimated 3.3 · 10^18 FLOPs — a fraction of its competitors' cost.
A self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequential operations, O(1), where a recurrent layer requires O(n).
Single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting, but quality also drops when too many heads are used.
Learned positional embeddings produce nearly identical results to the sinusoidal encoding; the sinusoidal version was chosen in the hope it would extrapolate to longer sequences.

A 4-layer Transformer reached 92.7 F1 on WSJ Section 23 in the semi-supervised setting without task-specific tuning, beating every previously reported model except the Recurrent Neural Network Grammar.
limitations: Self-attention costs O(n² · d) per layer; the paper concedes it is faster than a recurrent layer only while the sequence length n stays below the representation dimension d.
The restricted self-attention proposed for long sequences was never measured — it is explicitly left to future work.
The English-to-French result is reported inconsistently: the body of Section 6.1 says 41.0 BLEU while the abstract and Table 2 say 41.8.
Averaging attention-weighted positions reduces effective resolution; the paper claims multi-head attention counteracts this but never quantifies the compensation.
The interpretability claim is qualitative — phrased with 'could' and 'appear to' — and no numerical measure of interpretability is offered.
Evaluation covers two translation directions and a single parsing task, and the paper notes only a small number of hyperparameter experiments were run for parsing.
The training-cost FLOP figures were not measured but estimated by multiplying training time, GPU count and an assumed sustained throughput per GPU.

glossary.definition: The problem of mapping one sequence of symbols to another; machine translation is the canonical case.

sourceRef.excerpt: The dominant sequence transduction models are based on complex recurrent or convolutional neural networks that include an encoder and a decoder.

glossary.definition: A function mapping a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output computed as a weighted sum of the values, where each weight comes from the compatibility of the query with the corresponding key.

sourceRef.excerpt: An attention function can be described as mapping a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output, where the query, keys, values, and output are all vectors.

glossary.definition: An attention mechanism relating different positions of a single sequence in order to compute a representation of that sequence; also called intra-attention.

sourceRef.excerpt: Self-attention, sometimes called intra-attention is an attention mechanism relating different positions of a single sequence in order to compute a representation of the sequence.

glossary.definition: Projecting queries, keys and values h times through different learned linear projections into a lower dimension, running attention in parallel, then concatenating and projecting the results.

sourceRef.excerpt: Multi-head attention allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions. With a single attention head, averaging inhibits this.

glossary.definition: Sine and cosine vectors of the same dimension as the embeddings, added to them so that a model without recurrence still receives order information.

sourceRef.excerpt: we add "positional encodings" to the input embeddings at the bottoms of the encoder and decoder stacks

glossary.definition: The longest distance a forward or backward signal must travel between any two input or output positions; shorter paths make long-range dependencies easier to learn.

sourceRef.excerpt: The shorter these paths between any combination of positions in the input and output sequences, the easier it is to learn long-range dependencies

glossary.definition: A regulariser that leaves some uncertainty in the target distribution instead of concentrating it on a single point; here it hurt perplexity while improving BLEU.

sourceRef.excerpt: This hurts perplexity, as the model learns to be more unsure, but improves accuracy and BLEU score.

glossary.definition: Generating each symbol while consuming the previously generated symbols as additional input.

sourceRef.excerpt: At each step the model is auto-regressive [10], consuming the previously generated symbols as additional input when generating the next.

story.title: Attention Is Enough: The Architecture That Dropped Sequentiality
story.dek: How the Transformer removed recurrence, what it paid in exchange, and which numbers the paper actually proves — tracked page by page against the evidence.

sections.title: Sequentiality was the wall in front of scale
sections.body:
In 2017 the standard for sequence modelling was the recurrent network, and its core constraint was temporal rather than architectural: because the hidden state h_t depends on h_{t-1}, computation had to queue along the positions of the sequence. The paper names this plainly as a barrier to parallelisation, and notes that memory constraints also limit batching across examples at longer lengths, which is where the problem turns critical.

Convolutional alternatives — ByteNet, ConvS2S — brought parallelism at a different price: the number of operations required to relate two distant positions grew with the distance between them, linearly for ConvS2S and logarithmically for ByteNet. You had to sacrifice either sequentiality or the cheapness of long-range dependencies.

The Transformer's claim is that this dilemma can be removed entirely: connect any two positions with a constant number of operations.

sections.title: Six layers, three uses of attention, zero recurrence
sections.body:
The Transformer keeps the classic encoder-decoder skeleton but hollows it out and refills it. The encoder is six identical layers; each has two sub-layers, multi-head self-attention and a position-wise fully connected feed-forward network. Every sub-layer is wrapped in a residual connection followed by layer normalisation — which is why all sub-layers and the embedding layers must produce outputs of dimension d_model = 512.

The decoder is also six layers, but a third sub-layer is inserted between them: multi-head attention over the output of the encoder stack. This is the counterpart of encoder-decoder attention in classic seq2seq.

The critical detail is masking. In the decoder's self-attention sub-layer, looking at later positions is prevented. Combined with offsetting the output embeddings by one position, this guarantees that the prediction for position i depends only on known outputs at positions before i. That is how auto-regressive generation is preserved.

sections.title: Why the scaling was necessary
sections.body:
Attention itself is not new; the paper's contribution is making it the sole carrier and adding one correction that makes it work in practice. In Scaled Dot-Product Attention the query is dotted with every key, each result is divided by √d_k, softmax turns those into weights, and the values are summed with them.

The division is not cosmetic. Additive attention outperforms unscaled dot-product attention at larger d_k. The authors' explanation is offered as a supposition: for large d_k the dot products may grow large in magnitude and push softmax into a region where its gradients are extremely small. A footnote shows why that is expected — if the components are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, the dot product has variance d_k.

Dot product was preferred for an engineering reason: although the theoretical complexity is similar, it is much faster and more space-efficient in practice because it can be implemented with highly optimised matrix multiplication.

visual.caption: Scaled Dot-Product Attention: the paper's definition, term by term.

terms.label: Query matrix
terms.detail: All queries are packed into one matrix so they can be computed simultaneously (p. 4).

terms.label: Key matrix
terms.detail: d_k-dimensional vectors determining the query's compatibility with each position (p. 4).

terms.label: Value matrix
terms.detail: d_v-dimensional content vectors to be summed with the weights (p. 4).

terms.label: Scaling factor
terms.detail: A precaution against large d_k pushing softmax into its small-gradient region (p. 4).

terms.label: Weight normalisation
terms.detail: Turns compatibility scores into weights summing to 1; masked connections are set to −∞ (pp. 4-5).

steps: Take the dot product of the query with every key.
Divide each score by √d_k, to prevent gradient collapse at large d_k.
Mask forbidden connections by setting them to −∞ at the softmax input.
Apply softmax to obtain the weights.
Sum the values with those weights to produce the output.

sections.title: Table 1: what is won and what is paid
sections.body:
Table 1 is the paper's most honest table. It compares three criteria: computational complexity per layer, the minimum number of sequential operations required, and the maximum path length.

Self-attention wins outright on sequential operations and path length, O(1) on both, where a recurrent layer is O(n) on both. But the complexity column reverses it: self-attention is O(n² · d) against O(n · d²) for recurrence. The paper does not hide this trade-off; it states the condition under which self-attention is faster — the sequence length n must be smaller than the representation dimension d.

In the sentence-level translation setting of 2017 that condition usually held. What to do when it does not is left as an unmeasured suggestion: restricted self-attention over a neighbourhood of size r, at the cost of raising the path length to O(n/r). The authors' phrasing is explicit — they plan to investigate it in future work.

visual.caption: Layer types compared on three criteria; tone marks an advantage (high) or disadvantage (low) from self-attention's point of view.

sections.title: Two BLEU scores and a difference in cost
sections.body:
On WMT 2014 English-to-German, Transformer (big) scores 28.4 BLEU and beats the best previously reported models — ensembles included — by more than 2.0 BLEU. That a single model surpasses ensembles is the strongest part of the result.

The second axis is the striking one: cost. Even the base model beats every previously published model and ensemble, and does it at an estimated 3.3 · 10^18 FLOPs — most of its rivals in Table 2 sit between 10^19 and 10^21.

One caveat is required. Those FLOP figures were not measured. The paper says they were estimated by multiplying training time, the number of GPUs and an assumed sustained capacity per GPU. So while the cost comparison gives the right order of magnitude, it should not be read as a precise measurement.

sections.title: A recipe running from 12 hours to 3.5 days
sections.body:
Most of the training details are stated explicitly, which matters for reproducibility. On the data side, WMT 2014 English-German supplied about 4.5 million sentence pairs with a shared byte-pair vocabulary of roughly 37000 tokens; batches were formed to hold approximately 25000 source and 25000 target tokens.

The hardware was a single machine with 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs. The base model trained for 100,000 steps — about 12 hours — and the big model for 300,000 steps, or 3.5 days.

Optimisation used Adam under a warmup schedule: a linear rise over the first 4000 steps, then decay proportional to the inverse square root of the step number. Regularisation had two parts — dropout at P_drop = 0.1 on sub-layer outputs and on the sum of embeddings and position encodings, plus label smoothing of 0.1. Here too the paper shares an honest observation: label smoothing hurts perplexity but improves accuracy and BLEU.

sections.title: Which part was actually necessary
sections.body:
Table 3 measures how much each component carries, on the newstest2013 development set. Four findings stand out.

First, multi-head really helps, but not monotonically: single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU below the best setting, yet quality falls again when the head count is pushed too high. So h is a hyperparameter, not a free source of gains.

Second, shrinking d_k degrades quality. The paper draws from this that determining compatibility is not easy and that a more sophisticated compatibility function than the dot product might help.

Third, as expected: bigger models are better, and dropout is very helpful against overfitting.

Fourth, and most interesting — replacing the sinusoidal position encoding with learned positional embeddings gives nearly identical results. One of the paper's most iconic design details is, in terms of measured performance, not necessary; the reason it was chosen is an unmeasured hope about generalisation.

sections.title: What the paper concedes, and one inconsistency
sections.body:
The Transformer's impact is not in question, but three separate kinds of caution are required when reading this paper.

The first is an acknowledged limit: quadratic cost. Self-attention is faster than a recurrent layer only while n < d. The restricted attention proposed as the long-sequence remedy was never tried here.

The second is a difference in evidence level. Interpretability is not a result but a side benefit, presented with 'could' and 'appear to'. The justification for the √d_k scaling is likewise a supposition ('We suspect'), not a measured explanation of mechanism. The paper concedes that averaging reduces effective resolution and claims multi-head attention counteracts it, but the degree of compensation is never quantified.

The third is a direct inconsistency: the English-to-French result appears as 41.0 BLEU in the body of Section 6.1 and as 41.8 BLEU in the abstract and Table 2. Two different numbers for the same model. Anyone citing this paper should say which value they used; this project keeps both with their evidence and marks the relevant claim as needing review.

visual.caption: The paper's claims layered by strength of support; the top layer has the weakest backing.

items.label: Directly measured
items.detail: BLEU 28.4 (EN-DE), base model 27.3, parsing F1 92.7, the ablation differences — all measured on a test or development set.

items.label: Estimated
items.detail: The FLOP costs in Table 2, derived from time × GPU count × assumed throughput.

items.label: Hypothesis level
items.detail: The √d_k rationale ('We suspect') and the extrapolation advantage of sinusoidal encoding ('may allow') — unmeasured.

items.label: Inconsistently reported
items.detail: EN-FR BLEU: 41.0 in the body, 41.8 in the abstract and Table 2. Same model, two numbers.

closing.title: Why it is still read
closing.body: This paper is less an architecture proposal than the removal of a constraint: once sequential computation stopped being mandatory, the bottleneck on scaling moved from the architecture to the hardware. Read today, the most prescient part is the plan in the conclusion — extending the input and output to modalities beyond text, and investigating local, restricted attention for large inputs. Those two sentences describe much of the following decade's research agenda. Against that, the ground the paper measures is narrow: two translation directions and one parsing task. The Transformer's generality was not proved here; it was proved by what came after.

deepReport.title: Attention Is All You Need — Deep Review
deepReport.dek: Nine evidence-linked sections on where the contribution sits, how the mechanism works, how strong the experimental evidence is, what is inconsistent, and what reproduction would require.

sections.title: What the contribution is, and what it is not
sections.summary: The contribution is not inventing attention but making it the sole carrier, removing recurrence entirely, and showing that this works on two translation tasks.
analysis: Attention was in use before this paper, and Section 2 says so openly: with few exceptions it had been used together with a recurrent network. The core of the contribution is breaking that pairing — 'dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely'.

The second layer of contribution is the measurable one: improving quality and lowering cost at the same time. Both axes moving together makes the architectural change look like a gain rather than a trade. But as Table 1 shows, the trade does not vanish — it relocates, from sequential operations to quadratic memory.

The third contribution is the one the authors emphasise least and which lasted longest: the component list (multi-head attention, position encoding, residual plus LayerNorm, a warmup learning rate) became a standard for the models that followed. The paper does not present it as a standard; it reports it as a configuration that works.

It is worth being careful about scope: the paper does not claim the Transformer is a general-purpose representation learner. The claim is confined to sequence transduction, and the evidence of generalisation is a single additional task.

sections.title: Scaled dot-product attention: why this form
sections.summary: Dot product was chosen for speed and the √d_k scaling for gradient health; the paper presents the second justification explicitly as a hypothesis.
analysis: There are two common attention functions, additive and dot-product. The paper notes their theoretical complexity is similar but that dot product is much faster and more space-efficient in practice, because it can use highly optimised matrix multiplication. That is an implementation choice, not a modelling one.

The scaling is on the modelling side. Unscaled dot product falls behind additive attention at large d_k. The authors' explanation: the dot products may grow large in magnitude and push softmax into a region of extremely small gradients. The mood of the sentence matters — 'We suspect' — it is not offered as an established mechanism.

The footnote argument makes the hypothesis probabilistically plausible: if the components of q and k are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, the dot product has variance d_k, so dividing by √d_k pulls the variance back to unit scale. This is a motivation, not a derivation; the paper reports no direct comparison of scaled against unscaled in its own experiments, justifying it instead by reference to other work.

The practical consequence: √d_k is an unquestioned standard today, but in this paper its empirical basis is indirect. It follows from the derivation that when d_k changes, the scaling must change with it.

sections.title: Multi-head, masking and position information
sections.summary: Three structural decisions make the architecture work without recurrence; the evidential strength of the three differs.
analysis: Multi-head is not an increase in capacity but a redistribution. Because d_model = 512 is split across eight heads, each works at d_k = d_v = 64, and the paper notes the total cost stays comparable to single-head attention at full dimensionality. The gain is being able to attend to different representation subspaces at once; the paper says averaging in a single head inhibits this. The empirical support for that claim is the 0.9 BLEU difference in Table 3 row (A).

Masking is a correctness guarantee for auto-regressive generation. The implementation detail matters: forbidden connections are set to −∞ at the softmax input, so masking is embedded inside the attention function. Combined with offsetting the output embeddings by one position, this guarantees the prediction at position i depends only on positions before i. This is not a performance claim but a correctness condition.

Position encoding is the part of the architecture with the most fragile justification. The reason the sinusoidal version was chosen is not a measured advantage: Table 3 row (E) shows learned embeddings give nearly identical results. The choice rests on the hope of extrapolating to sequences longer than those seen in training, and the paper does not test that hope.

Read together, the skeleton emerges: attention carries the 'what', masking the 'when', and position encoding the 'where'. Removing recurrence is possible only because of that third piece — without it, order information never reaches the model at all.

sections.title: How strong the translation evidence is
sections.summary: The headline results are reported on two WMT 2014 tasks; the quality claim is strong, the cost claim weaker because it rests on estimation.
analysis: The English-German result is the paper's soundest evidence: Transformer (big) beats the best previously reported models, ensembles included, by more than 2.0 BLEU. A single model beating ensembles is a meaningful threshold, because ensembles usually enjoy an artificial advantage over single models.

The base model's performance carries a separate argument: at 27.3 BLEU it beats every previously published model and ensemble at a fraction of their cost. That shows the result does not come from scale alone — the architectural change itself contributes.

The cost claim sits in a different evidence class. The FLOP figures in Table 2 were not measured; they were estimated by multiplying training time, GPU count and an assumed sustained single-precision capacity per GPU. The capacity values used (9.5 TFLOPS for the P100, for instance) are given in a footnote. The method suffices for comparing orders of magnitude but cannot support small differences between two models.

The evaluation protocol has details worth noting too: the base model averages the last 5 checkpoints and the big model the last 20, with beam size 4 and length penalty α = 0.6 selected on the development set. These are standard practices, but whether the compared models used the same protocol is not clear from the paper.

sections.title: What the ablations prove
sections.summary: Table 3 is the only evidence supporting component-level causal claims; because it is measured on the development set without checkpoint averaging, it must be read separately from the headline table.
analysis: The ablation protocol differs from the headline results in two ways: measurements are on the newstest2013 development set, and no checkpoint averaging is used. So the BLEU values in Table 3 cannot be compared directly with Table 2. The paper also warns explicitly that the perplexities are per word-piece and should not be compared with per-word figures.

Row (A) supplies causal support for multi-head: computation is held constant while only the head count and d_k, d_v vary. A single head costs 0.9 BLEU, and 32 heads also cause a decline. This shows h is a hyperparameter that needs optimising.

Row (B) offers a more interesting observation: quality degrades when d_k is reduced, and the paper concludes from this that determining compatibility is not easy and that a more sophisticated compatibility function than the dot product may be beneficial. That is the paper's clearest self-criticism of its own design choice.

Row (E) shows one part of the architecture to be unnecessary: learned positional embeddings are nearly identical to sinusoidal encoding. This finding is direct evidence against later accounts that present sinusoidal encoding as a mandatory Transformer component.

One important axis the ablations do not cover: the contribution of residual connections and layer normalisation is never measured. These components are critical to scaling the architecture in depth, yet the paper does not ablate them.

sections.title: Inconsistencies and gaps in the evidence
sections.summary: The paper contains one numerical inconsistency, several hypothesis-level justifications and one unmeasured compensation claim; none invalidates the headline result, but all affect how it should be cited.
analysis: The most concrete problem is the English-French BLEU. The body of Section 6.1 says the big model reaches 41.0 BLEU while the abstract and Table 2 give 41.8 for the same model. Still present in the seventh arXiv version, this inconsistency obliges any citing work to state which value it used. This project marks the relevant claim as needing review and keeps both sources.

The second gap is a confusion of evidence levels. The justification for √d_k ('We suspect'), the extrapolation advantage of sinusoidal encoding ('may allow') and interpretability ('could yield', 'appear to exhibit') are all written in the hypothetical mood. Later literature frequently relayed these as established findings; the text of the paper does not support that.

The third is a compensation claim. Section 2 concedes that averaging attention-weighted positions reduces effective resolution and says multi-head attention counteracts it. But no experiment measures how much of the loss is recovered; Table 3 row (A) shows only the BLEU effect of head count, not the resolution loss directly.

The fourth is scope. The paper states plainly that only a small number of hyperparameter experiments were run for the parsing task. That is an honest disclosure, but it also means those results are not the product of a systematic search, and the generalisation claim should be read with corresponding restraint.

sections.title: Reproduction: what is given and what is not
sections.summary: Most hyperparameters and the training regime are reported explicitly and the code is available in tensor2tensor; a few details still cannot be recovered from the paper.
analysis: What is given is fairly comprehensive for a reproduction: datasets and sizes (EN-DE ~4.5M sentence pairs with a shared ~37000-token BPE vocabulary; EN-FR 36M sentences with 32000 word-pieces), batch size (~25000 source + ~25000 target tokens), hardware (8 P100s, one machine), step counts and durations, optimisation (Adam β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.98, ϵ = 10⁻⁹, warmup 4000), regularisation (P_drop = 0.1, ϵ_ls = 0.1) and inference settings (beam 4, α = 0.6, checkpoint averaging).

Code availability adds a separate guarantee: the paper states the training and evaluation code is in the tensor2tensor repository, which means differences between the description and the code can be audited. The paper does not say which version produced which result.

There are omissions. Random seeds and repetition counts are not reported, so it is impossible to judge how meaningful a difference like the 0.9 BLEU in Table 3 is against run-to-run variance. The big EN-FR model is noted as using a dropout rate of 0.1 instead of 0.3, but no reason for the exception is given.

One more practical risk: the GPU capacity assumptions underlying the FLOP estimate (2.8, 3.7, 6.0 and 9.5 TFLOPS for K80, K40, M40 and P100 respectively) do not hold on modern hardware. Repeating the cost comparison today would require redefining the method itself.
In sum, reproducing the translation results is reasonably feasible; statistically validating the ablation differences is not possible with the information the paper provides.

sections.title: The door left open by quadratic cost
sections.summary: The paper concedes its own solution will not work on long sequences and leaves the remedy to future work; that became one of the most productive research veins of the following decade.
analysis: The most cited row of Table 1 is self-attention's O(n² · d) cost. The paper presents it not as a defect but as a condition: self-attention is faster than a recurrent layer when n < d. In the sentence-level translation setting of 2017, with d = 512 and typical sentence lengths, that condition usually held.

What happens when it does not hold is left as a suggestion: restricted self-attention over a neighbourhood of size r reduces the layer cost to O(r · n · d) but raises the maximum path length to O(n/r). The authors write that they plan to investigate this — meaning there is no measured result in this paper.

That open door matters because most modern usage violates precisely the paper's condition: long context windows push n far above d. The paper's own analysis predicts that in this regime self-attention has no advantage left over a recurrent layer.

The plan in the conclusion confirms this reading: the authors write that they intend to investigate local and restricted attention mechanisms to handle large inputs and outputs such as images, audio and video efficiently, and to make generation less sequential.

sections.title: The generalisation evidence and its limits
sections.summary: The parsing experiment is the only direct evidence that the architecture is not translation-specific; strong, but not enough on its own to support a claim of general purpose.
analysis: English constituency parsing is a demanding choice of test: the output is subject to strong structural constraints and is significantly longer than the input. The paper also notes that recurrent seq2seq models had not reached state-of-the-art results in small-data regimes — so this is not a domain where a recurrence-free model is naturally advantaged.

The results are good: a 4-layer Transformer reaches 91.3 F1 with only the 40K-sentence WSJ set and 92.7 F1 in the semi-supervised setting, beating every previously reported model except the Recurrent Neural Network Grammar. The paper also stresses that it beats the BerkeleyParser even when trained on WSJ alone.

The limits of that evidence are equally clear. This is a single additional task, and the paper states outright that only a small number of hyperparameter experiments were run; all other parameters were taken unchanged from the EN-DE base translation model. That argues for the robustness of the result — it works well without tuning — but not for breadth of scope.

The honest reading is therefore: the Transformer was shown to generalise beyond translation within sequence transduction. A claim of general-purpose representation learning does not appear in this paper and is not supported by the evidence here; that claim belongs to the literature that followed.

openQuestions: Which is the correct English-French result — the 41.0 in the body or the 41.8 in the abstract and Table 2 — and what evaluation difference explains the gap?
What quality is actually lost when restricted (r-neighbourhood) self-attention is applied, and beyond what n does the O(n/r) path-length increase become a practical problem?
How could the extent to which multi-head attention compensates for the resolution loss from averaging be measured directly?
Are differences such as the 0.9 BLEU in Table 3 statistically meaningful against seed variance, and can that even be assessed given the paper reports no repetition count?
Can the extrapolation advantage claimed for sinusoidal position encoding be verified in a direct experiment against learned embeddings?
Had residual connections and layer normalisation been ablated, what share of the architecture's ability to scale in depth would they have accounted for?

technicalAppendix.title: Technical Appendix: Equations, Algorithm and Complexity
technicalAppendix.overview: This appendix contains only equations the paper writes explicitly, algorithm steps it describes, and the complexity figures given in Table 1. The code sketches are explanatory pseudocode; the paper publishes no equivalent runnable code, so what is represented here is the described flow rather than an implementation.

equations.label: Scaled Dot-Product Attention (Equation 1)
equations.explanation: Query-key dot products are scaled by √d_k, turned into weights by softmax, and used to sum the values. The scaling guards against softmax drifting into its small-gradient region at large d_k.

variables.meaning: Key/query dimension; 64 in the base model

equations.label: Multi-Head Attention
equations.expression: MultiHead(Q, K, V) = Concat(head₁, ..., head_h) Wᴼ,  head_i = Attention(Q Wᵢᑫ, K Wᵢᴷ, V Wᵢⱽ)
equations.explanation: Queries, keys and values are projected h times through different learned linear projections down to d_k, d_k and d_v; attention runs in parallel and the outputs are concatenated and projected again. Because the per-head dimension is reduced, the total cost stays comparable to a single full-dimension head.

variables.meaning: Number of parallel heads; 8 in this work
Projection matrices of shape R^(d_model × d_k)
Projection matrix of shape R^(d_model × d_v)
Output projection of shape R^(h·d_v × d_model)

equations.label: Position-wise feed-forward network (Equation 2)
equations.expression: FFN(x) = max(0, x W₁ + b₁) W₂ + b₂
equations.explanation: Two linear transformations with a ReLU in between, applied to each position separately and identically. The paper also describes it as two convolutions with kernel size 1. Parameters are shared across positions but differ from layer to layer.

variables.meaning: The d_model-dimensional representation of a single position

equations.label: Sinusoidal position encoding
equations.explanation: Each dimension corresponds to a sinusoid, with wavelengths forming a geometric progression from 2π to 10000·2π. The stated reason for the choice is that for any fixed offset k, PE(pos+k) can be represented as a linear function of PE(pos), which the authors hypothesised would make attending by relative position easier.

variables.meaning: Dimension index within the encoding vector

equations.label: Warmup learning rate schedule (Equation 3)
equations.explanation: The learning rate rises linearly over the first warmup_steps and then decays with the inverse square root of the step number. This work uses warmup_steps = 4000.

variables.meaning: Model dimension, used here as a scale factor

algorithmSteps.label: 1. Combine embeddings with position information
algorithmSteps.detail: Turn input and output tokens into learned embeddings of dimension d_model = 512; the embedding weights are multiplied by √d_model. Add sinusoidal position encodings to the embeddings at the bottom of the encoder and decoder stacks.

algorithmSteps.label: 2. Apply an encoder layer (×6)
algorithmSteps.detail: Run multi-head self-attention, then the position-wise feed-forward network. Each sub-layer output is added through a residual connection and normalised, in the form LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)).

algorithmSteps.label: 3. Split into heads and compute attention in parallel
algorithmSteps.detail: Project Q, K, V through h = 8 different learned projections down to d_k = d_v = 64, compute scaled dot-product attention in each head in parallel, then concatenate and project the outputs with Wᴼ.

algorithmSteps.label: 4. Mask the look-ahead in the decoder
algorithmSteps.detail: In the decoder's self-attention sub-layer, set the softmax inputs corresponding to forbidden connections to −∞. Combined with offsetting the output embeddings by one position, position i stays dependent only on positions before i.

algorithmSteps.label: 5. Run encoder-decoder attention
algorithmSteps.detail: Take queries from the previous decoder layer and keys and values from the encoder stack's output. Every decoder position can then attend to all positions of the input sequence.

algorithmSteps.label: 6. Produce the output probabilities
algorithmSteps.detail: Convert the decoder output into next-token probabilities through a linear transformation and softmax; this weight matrix is shared with the two embedding layers.

algorithmSteps.label: 7. Train with the warmup schedule
algorithmSteps.detail: Run Adam with β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.98, ϵ = 10⁻⁹; raise the learning rate linearly over the first 4000 steps, then decay it with the inverse square root of the step number.

algorithmSteps.label: 8. Apply regularisation
algorithmSteps.detail: Apply dropout to each sub-layer output before the residual addition and normalisation, and also to the sum of embeddings and position encodings (P_drop = 0.1). Use label smoothing of 0.1 during training.

codeSketches.title: Scaled dot-product attention (explanatory pseudocode)
codeSketches.code:
def scaled_dot_product_attention(Q, K, V, mask=None):
    # Q: (n_q, d_k), K: (n_k, d_k), V: (n_k, d_v)
    scores = Q @ K.T                 # uyum skorlari
    scores = scores / sqrt(d_k)      # Denklem (1): olcekleme
    if mask is not None:
        # yasak baglantilar softmax girisinde -inf yapilir
        scores = where(mask, scores, -inf)
    weights = softmax(scores, axis=-1)
    return weights @ V               # degerlerin agirlikli toplami
codeSketches.explanation: A one-to-one counterpart of the flow described in Section 3.2.1. As stated in Section 3.2.3, masking is applied inside the attention function by assigning −∞ at the softmax input. This pseudocode is explanatory; the paper publishes no equivalent code.

implementationNotes: Every sub-layer and embedding layer must output dimension d_model = 512; residual connections force this equality.
Masking is not a separate step but is applied inside the attention function by assigning −∞ at the softmax input.
Embedding weights are shared between the two embedding layers and the pre-softmax linear transformation, and are multiplied by √d_model in the embedding layers.
The choice d_k = d_v = d_model / h keeps the cost constant; break that relation while changing h and comparison with Table 3 row (A) becomes invalid.

primer.title: Before you read this paper
primer.overview: The paper assumes six concepts and explains none of them. The order below follows the prerequisite chain: every concept comes before the one that depends on it. Each entry gives the intuition first, then the formal definition, then exactly why this paper needs it.

concepts.intuition: You multiply two vectors element by element and add the results. The number you get measures how much the two point in the same direction: large and positive when aligned, near zero when perpendicular, negative when opposed. It is a similarity score.
concepts.whyItMatters: The whole of attention rests on this. How much a query attends to a key is decided by the dot product between them. That is why the paper calls its attention function "Scaled Dot-Product Attention".

concepts.intuition: You have a list of arbitrary numbers and want to turn them into positive weights that sum to one. Softmax exponentiates each and divides by the total. Large numbers take a disproportionately large share — it behaves like a soft maximum.
concepts.whyItMatters: Dot-product scores are raw numbers; softmax turns them into "how much should I look at each position" weights. Its critical behaviour is this: as the inputs grow, the output piles onto a single position and the gradients nearly vanish. That is exactly the reason the paper divides by √d_k.

concepts.intuition: Variance measures how far a random value spreads from its mean. Add independent values and the variances add: sum d_k independent terms each of variance 1 and the total has variance d_k, so a standard deviation of √d_k.
concepts.whyItMatters: This is the entire argument in the paper's footnote. As d_k grows the dot products typically grow on the scale of √d_k and softmax saturates. Dividing by √d_k pulls the spread back to unit scale. The scaling is not cosmetic; it follows directly from this calculation.

concepts.intuition: The model works with numbers, not words. Each token is represented by a learned vector of fixed length, tuned during training so that tokens with similar meaning land near one another.
concepts.whyItMatters: In the Transformer every sub-layer and every embedding layer must output the same dimension (512), so that residual connections can be added. This constraint shows up everywhere in the architecture.

concepts.intuition: In a recurrent network the hidden state at position t depends on t−1. To process word 500 you must first have finished 499. The computation is inherently queued — however many GPUs you have.
concepts.whyItMatters: This is why the paper exists. Because the Transformer breaks that dependency it can parallelise within a training example and reach state of the art in twelve hours on eight GPUs.

concepts.intuition: A residual connection adds a sub-layer's output back to its input: LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)). The layer then answers "what should I add to the current representation" rather than "produce a representation from scratch". Normalisation keeps values on a fixed scale so deep stacks stay trainable.
concepts.whyItMatters: This is why six-layer stacks train at all. The paper does not ablate either component, so their contribution is unmeasured — but without them this depth is not practical.

concepts.intuition: The encoder turns the input sequence into a sequence of representations. The decoder consults those and produces the output one token at a time, feeding each token it has generated back in as input. That is auto-regressive generation.
concepts.whyItMatters: You need this to see why masking in the decoder is mandatory: if the model can see the future during training, it comes to rely on information it will not have at inference. Masking is a correctness condition, not a speed optimisation.

derivations.title: Where dividing by √d_k comes from
derivations.goal: Derive, step by step, the scaling rationale the paper gives in a single sentence, starting from the probabilistic argument in its footnote.

steps.rationale: The starting point: the compatibility score between a query and a key is a sum of d_k terms.
The paper's footnote assumption: the components are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1. This is an assumption, not a proof — it does not hold exactly in a trained model.

steps.plain: Var(q · k) = Σ Var(q_i k_i) = d_k
steps.rationale: Variances add for independent variables. With d_k terms the total variance is exactly d_k.
Standard deviation is the square root of variance. So the typical magnitude of the scores grows with √d_k, not d_k — this is the source of the scaling factor.

steps.plain: as |x| grows, softmax collapses onto a single position
steps.rationale: As the inputs grow, the exponential overwhelmingly favours the largest term. The output becomes almost one-hot, and in that region softmax has almost no gradient — what the paper calls 'extremely small gradients'.
Dividing by √d_k fixes the variance at 1 regardless of d_k. Softmax then sees inputs at the same scale whatever d_k is, and does not saturate.

numericExample.setup: The paper's configuration: d_k = 64. Suppose the typical gap between two keys' scores is on the order of a standard deviation, that is √64 = 8.
walkthrough: Without scaling: a score gap of 8 → softmax weight ≈ 1/(1+e⁻⁸) ≈ 0.9997
The model is looking at essentially one position; the gradients for the others are vanishingly small.
With scaling: the gap becomes 8/√64 = 1 → softmax weight ≈ 1/(1+e⁻¹) ≈ 0.731
That is a healthy distribution producing stable gradients.
numericExample.result: At d_k = 64 the scaling pulls a single weight from 0.9997 down to 0.731. As d_k grows the unscaled version sticks to 1 while the scaled one stays constant. You can slide through this yourself in the "Why the scaling is necessary" playground.

derivations.title: How multi-head attention preserves the dimensions
derivations.goal: Show through shape tracking why splitting into h heads does not change the total cost.

steps.rationale: The input: n positions, each of dimension d_model = 512.
Every head has its own projection matrices. We choose d_k = d_v = d_model/h = 512/8 = 64.
Each head computes attention in a 64-dimensional subspace instead of the full dimension. Cost per head drops by a factor of 8.
The critical point: h·d_v = 8·64 = 512 = d_model. Concatenating the heads brings us back to exactly the dimension we started from.
The final projection mixes what the heads found. Since the dimension is unchanged, the residual connection can be added directly — the rest of the architecture notices nothing.

walkthrough: Single head at full dimension: one attention computation over 512-dimensional Q, K, V.
Multi-head: eight attention computations at 64 dimensions.
Attention cost scales linearly with dimension, so 8 × 64 = 512: the total is the same.
numericExample.result: Multi-head is not added capacity but a redistribution of the same budget. The gain comes from being able to attend to different representation subspaces at once — measured in Table 3 row (A) as 0.9 BLEU.

derivations.title: The warmup learning rate schedule
derivations.goal: Show why Equation (3) first rises and then falls, and exactly where the breakpoint sits.

steps.rationale: Equation (3) from the paper. A min of two branches: whichever is smaller applies.

steps.plain: while step << warmup the second branch is smaller
steps.rationale: Early in training the second branch is selected and grows LINEARLY with step. This is what stops the model taking large steps while it is still randomly initialised.

steps.plain: at step = warmup the two branches are equal
steps.rationale: The breakpoint is exactly step = warmup — step 4000 in this work. Because the two branches are equal there, the schedule is continuous; there is no jump.
After that the first branch takes over and the learning rate decays with the inverse square root of the step number — classic convergence behaviour.

interactives.title: Why the scaling is necessary
interactives.description: Slide d_k. In the unscaled version a single attention weight rushes to 1 — the region where gradients vanish. Divided by √d_k it stays constant regardless of d_k. The comparison shows the case where the score gap between two keys equals the typical spread (√d_k).
interactives.paperAnchor: The paper uses d_k = 64 (d_model = 512, h = 8). The scaling rationale is presented as a HYPOTHESIS ('We suspect'), not a measured result.

interactives.title: When self-attention becomes expensive
interactives.description: Run the two rows of Table 1 side by side. Self-attention is O(n²·d), a recurrent layer O(n·d²). While n < d self-attention is cheap; once n passes d the curves cross and the advantage reverses. The y-axis is logarithmic.
interactives.paperAnchor: The paper uses d_model = 512 and states explicitly that self-attention is faster than a recurrent layer only while n < d. The point n = d is that threshold; once the ratio passes 1 the paper's condition is violated.

interactives.title: Attention weights, step by step
interactives.description: The six steps of Scaled Dot-Product Attention. The grid shows the weight each query gives each key in a four-token sentence; darker means heavier. The numbers are ILLUSTRATIVE — the paper publishes no example attention matrix; the mechanism shown belongs to the paper, the values serve the explanation.

stageNodes.label: QKᵀ
stageNodes.detail: A raw compatibility score for every query-key pair

stageNodes.label: ÷ √d_k

frames.label: Split the input three ways
frames.caption: The same input goes through three different learned projections: query (what am I looking for), key (what do I have), value (what do I give if found).

frames.label: Compute the raw scores
frames.caption: Every query is dotted with every key. The values can grow freely — the typical spread here is on the order of √d_k.

frames.label: Scale by √d_k
frames.caption: All scores are divided by √64 = 8. The range narrows and softmax no longer works in its saturated region.

frames.label: Mask the future
frames.caption: In the decoder position i may only see positions before i. Forbidden cells are set to −∞ at the softmax input; shown here as 0.

frames.label: Apply softmax
frames.caption: Each row becomes a weight distribution summing to 1. The lower-triangular structure holds: no position gives weight to the future.

frames.label: Sum the values by weight
frames.caption: The final step: each position's output is the sum of the value vectors scaled by the weights. All of this happens for every position at once, as a single matrix multiplication — no sequentiality.

interactives.title: How information flows from encoder to decoder
interactives.description: The three uses of attention and where each sits in the stack. Watch which component is active at each step.

stageNodes.label: Input + position
stageNodes.detail: Embedding and sinusoidal encoding are summed

stageNodes.label: Encoder self-attention
stageNodes.detail: Every position may attend to all input positions

stageNodes.label: Encoder FFN
stageNodes.detail: Two position-wise linear transformations with ReLU in between

stageNodes.label: Encoder-decoder attention
stageNodes.detail: Queries from the decoder, keys and values from the encoder

frames.label: The input is prepared
frames.caption: Because there is no recurrence, order must be injected separately: sinusoidal position encodings are ADDED to the embeddings, not concatenated.

frames.label: The encoder stack runs (×6)
frames.caption: Self-attention and the feed-forward network, each wrapped in a residual connection and layer normalisation, repeated six times. All positions are processed in parallel.

frames.label: The decoder looks at its own past
frames.caption: Masked self-attention: position i may depend only on known outputs at positions before i. This is how auto-regression is preserved.

frames.label: The decoder looks at the input
frames.caption: The third sub-layer: queries come from the previous decoder layer, keys and values from the encoder stack's output. This is the counterpart of classic seq2seq attention.

frames.label: A token is produced
frames.caption: The output is turned into probabilities through weights shared with the embedding matrix. The generated token is then fed back and the loop continues.

quiz.title: Check your understanding
quiz.intro: Ten questions. After each answer you can see which claim and which page it rests on. The correct answers sit openly in the JSON — this is a self-check, not an exam.

questions.prompt: What is the paper's central claim about the Transformer?

options.label: Dispensing with recurrence and convolution entirely and relying only on attention
options.explanation: The abstract's own words: 'dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely'.

options.label: Inventing the attention mechanism
options.explanation: Attention predates the paper, as Section 2 acknowledges. The novelty is making attention the sole carrier.

options.label: Showing that larger models can be trained
options.explanation: The emphasis is architecture rather than scale; even the base model beats its rivals at a fraction of the cost.

questions.prompt: According to Table 1, what is the per-layer computational complexity of a self-attention layer?

options.label: O(n² · d)
options.explanation: Table 1, page 6. It grows with the SQUARE of the sequence length — the paper's acknowledged central trade-off.

options.label: O(n · d²)
options.explanation: That is the cost of a recurrent layer.

options.label: O(n log n)
options.explanation: No such row appears in the paper.

questions.prompt: When is self-attention faster than a recurrent layer?

options.label: When the sequence length n is smaller than the representation dimension d
options.explanation: The paper states this condition explicitly (pp. 6-7). On long contexts the condition breaks and the advantage disappears.

options.label: Always
options.explanation: The paper makes no such claim; it states the condition itself.

options.label: Only on GPUs
options.explanation: The comparison is asymptotic and hardware-independent.

questions.prompt: At what evidence level does the paper justify dividing dot products by √d_k?

options.label: A hypothesis — the paper says 'We suspect' and offers no measurement
options.explanation: Page 4. The footnote gives a probabilistic motivation, but no direct comparison of scaled against unscaled is reported here.

options.label: A result measured by ablation
options.explanation: Table 3 ablates head count, d_k, model size and position encoding — not the scaling factor.

options.label: A mathematical theorem
options.explanation: The variance argument in the footnote is a motivation, not a derivation or proof.

questions.prompt: Which of these are true of multi-head attention?

options.label: It uses h = 8 heads with d_k = d_v = 64
options.explanation: Page 5: d_k = d_v = d_model/h = 512/8 = 64.

options.label: Total computational cost stays comparable to single-head at full dimensionality
options.explanation: Because the per-head dimension is divided by h, the total stays constant — the paper states this explicitly.

options.label: Increasing the head count monotonically improves quality
options.explanation: Table 3 row (A): with too many heads quality FALLS again. h is a hyperparameter to be tuned.

options.label: Single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting
options.explanation: Table 3 row (A), page 9.

questions.prompt: Sinusoidal position encoding is measurably better than learned positional embeddings.

options.label: False
options.explanation: Table 3 row (E): the two versions give NEARLY IDENTICAL results. The sinusoidal version was preferred in the HOPE that it would generalise to longer sequences — a hope that was never tested.

options.label: True
options.explanation: The paper does not show this; it reports nearly identical results.

questions.prompt: What does masking in the decoder accomplish?

options.label: It guarantees the prediction at position i depends only on positions before i
options.explanation: Page 3. This is not a speed optimisation but a CORRECTNESS condition for auto-regressive generation.

options.label: It reduces memory
options.explanation: Masking sets forbidden entries to −∞ at the softmax input; memory is not the goal.

options.label: It speeds up training
options.explanation: The goal is not speed but preventing the model from seeing the future.

questions.prompt: How were the training-cost (FLOPs) figures in Table 2 obtained?

options.label: Estimated: time × GPU count × assumed capacity per GPU
options.explanation: Page 8. These are estimates, not measurements; adequate for comparing orders of magnitude but not small differences.

options.label: Measured directly with a profiler
options.explanation: The paper performs no such measurement.

options.label: Taken from the hardware vendor's report
options.explanation: The capacity figures are given as assumptions in a footnote; the costs are computed by the authors.

questions.prompt: The restricted self-attention proposed for long sequences was measured in this paper.

options.label: False
options.explanation: Page 7: 'We plan to investigate this approach further in future work.' There is a proposal, but no measurement.

options.label: True
options.explanation: It has a row in Table 1 but no experimental result is reported.

questions.prompt: What evidence of generalisation beyond translation does the paper offer?

options.label: English constituency parsing: a 4-layer model reaching 92.7 F1 in the semi-supervised setting
options.explanation: Table 4, page 10. Obtained without task-specific tuning; it is the only additional task.

options.label: Image classification
options.explanation: There is no vision experiment here; it appears only as a future plan in the conclusion.

options.label: Language modelling
options.explanation: The paper reports no language modelling result.

applicationGuide.title: Using it in your own project
applicationGuide.overview: You do not need to write a Transformer from scratch today. But knowing why each decision was made changes how you pick your own configuration. Every value below comes from the paper — there are no invented defaults. The code sketches are EXPLANATORY, not runnable library code.

recipe.detail: Choose d_model first, then h so that it divides evenly. Preserve the relation d_k = d_v = d_model/h; break it and the total cost no longer stays constant, which invalidates any comparison with the paper's ablations.

code.source:
d_model = 512      # makale: temel model
h = 8              # makale: paralel baslik sayisi
assert d_model % h == 0
d_k = d_v = d_model // h   # = 64
d_ff = 4 * d_model         # makale: 2048

recipe.step: Tie the scaling to d_k, do not hard-code it
recipe.detail: The 1/√d_k factor depends on d_k. Change the head dimension and the scaling must change with it; a hard-coded 0.125 (that is, 1/√64) turns into a silent bug.

code.source:
scores = (Q @ K.transpose(-2, -1)) / math.sqrt(d_k)
# DOGRU: d_k'ye bagli
# YANLIS: scores * 0.125  -> d_k degisince bozulur

recipe.step: Put the mask INSIDE the attention function
recipe.detail: Masking is not zeroing after softmax. Forbidden connections must be set to −∞ at the softmax INPUT; zero them afterwards and the rows no longer sum to 1 and the weights are wrong.

code.source:
scores = scores.masked_fill(causal_mask == 0, float('-inf'))
weights = scores.softmax(dim=-1)   # satir toplami = 1
# YANLIS: weights = scores.softmax(-1) * causal_mask

recipe.step: Use the warmup learning rate schedule
recipe.detail: Training a Transformer with a fixed learning rate is a classic failure mode. Equation (3) rises linearly for the first warmup_steps and then decays with step^-0.5; the breakpoint is exactly step = warmup.

recipe.step: Select checkpoints on BLEU, not perplexity
recipe.detail: Label smoothing deliberately hurts perplexity. The paper says so outright: 'This hurts perplexity ... but improves accuracy and BLEU score.' Pick your best checkpoint by validation perplexity and you will pick the wrong model.

hyperparameters.name: d_model
hyperparameters.guidance: Table 3 row (C): dropping to 256 takes BLEU from 25.8 to 24.5; raising to 1024 lifts it to 26.0. Bigger helps, with diminishing returns.

hyperparameters.name: h (head count)
hyperparameters.guidance: A single head costs 0.9 BLEU; 32 heads also degrade. The band between 8 and 16 works best. Not monotonic — tune it.

hyperparameters.name: d_ff
hyperparameters.guidance: Usually taken as 4·d_model. Raising it to 4096 lifts BLEU to 26.2 but pushes the parameter count to 90M.

hyperparameters.name: warmup_steps
hyperparameters.guidance: This value is given as a single setting and never swept. If your total step count differs greatly from 100K, consider scaling proportionally — but the paper offers no basis for that, so measure it on your own validation set.

hyperparameters.name: P_drop
hyperparameters.guidance: Table 3 row (D): turning dropout off takes BLEU from 25.8 to 24.6. Smaller datasets may need a higher value.

pitfalls.symptom: Training diverges or the loss becomes NaN in the first few thousand steps
pitfalls.cause: A fixed learning rate with no warmup. The model takes large steps while still randomly initialised.
pitfalls.fix: Apply the warmup schedule from Equation (3); the learning rate should rise linearly over the first 4000 steps.

pitfalls.symptom: Attention weights are almost one-hot and the model is not learning
pitfalls.cause: The √d_k scaling is missing or tied to the wrong dimension. Scores grow on the order of √d_k and push softmax into saturation.
pitfalls.fix: Tie the scaling to d_k. You can see the effect by sliding d_k in the "Why the scaling is necessary" playground.

pitfalls.symptom: Validation perplexity improves while BLEU falls
pitfalls.cause: Label smoothing hurts perplexity by design; the two metrics do not move together.
pitfalls.fix: Select checkpoints by BLEU, as the paper does.

pitfalls.symptom: Memory blows up on long documents
pitfalls.cause: Self-attention costs O(n²·d). The paper's advantage condition (n < d) is violated in long contexts.
pitfalls.fix: The paper proposes restricted attention for this case but never measures it. In practice look at chunking, sparse attention, or the efficient-attention variants developed after this paper.

pitfalls.symptom: My ablation numbers do not match the paper's
pitfalls.cause: Table 3 was measured on the development set (newstest2013) WITHOUT checkpoint averaging; Table 2 was measured on the test set with averaging.
pitfalls.fix: Check which table you are comparing against. The two are not directly comparable, and the paper warns about this explicitly.

whenNotToUse: When the sequence length markedly exceeds the representation dimension: the paper's own analysis says self-attention loses its advantage over a recurrent layer in that regime.
On very small datasets without task-specific tuning: the paper notes that even its parsing experiments involved only a small number of hyperparameter trials.

When sequential generation latency is critical: the Transformer parallelises training, but inference still emits one token at a time — the paper leaves 'making generation less sequential' to future work.
When carrying the paper's numbers to another model family: all results are specific to 2017 hardware and these datasets, and the FLOP estimates do not hold on today's hardware.
